Note: there is no Other Half taproom inside Industry City itself; this Centre St flagship is the closest Other Half location and acts as the beer-anchor counterpart to Brooklyn Kura's sake brewery.

name: The Gutter L.E.S.
desc: Manhattan sibling of the Williamsburg dive: 12 bowling lanes, pub, kitchen, and pinball arcade.
longDesc: The Lower East Side outpost of Brooklyn's Gutter brand opened in September 2023 with 12 bowling lanes, a full bar and kitchen, big TVs, and a pinball/arcade nook (Time Out, Brooklyn Paper). Lanes run $42 per half-hour ($50 premium) plus $8 shoes; minors allowed with adults until 7pm, 21+ after. A useful comparison piece to the Williamsburg original for nightlife/arcade vibes, though it's Manhattan-only and not drive-friendly from Industry City.
notes: Manhattan-only sibling — NOT in the 10-25 min IC drive radius (~30 min via Manhattan Bridge, parking is brutal on weekends in LES). Included for brand comparison vs the Williamsburg Gutter. 12 lanes, full bar + kitchen + pinball arcade (Time Out). Lane pricing $42/30min, $50 premium, $8 shoes, $4 socks (Yelp). Minors with adults until 7pm, 21+ after (gutterbarbowl.com). Opened Sept 2023 as expansion of the OG Williamsburg dive (Brooklyn Paper).

name: Best Pizza
desc: Frank Pinello's wood-fired classic NY slice shop — perfect pre-bowling stop before The Gutter.
longDesc: Opened in 2010 by Frank Pinello (host of Vice's 'The Pizza Show') in a converted Williamsburg bakery, Best Pizza uses a century-old wood-burning oven to turn out the platonic NY slice: plain, grandma, white, and a rotating special. No-frills counter, exposed brick, cash-or-card, and a 4-minute drive from The Gutter bowling alley — making it the natural cheap-eats anchor for a Williamsburg evening track.
notes: Pivoted from the original 'Frost Pizzeria' topic — Frost Restaurant at 193 Frost St (the old-school Italian sit-down spot, not a pizzeria) is listed as CLOSED on Yelp as of April 2026 (yelp.com/biz/frost-restaurant-brooklyn). Anna Maria Pizza at 179 Bedford, the other obvious old-school slice candidate, was replaced by Little Italy Pizza in June 2023 (northbrooklyndispatch.com). Best Pizza (33 Havemeyer St, Brooklyn, NY 11211) is the surviving classic NY slice anchor in this micro-cluster — sliceblog.com calls Pinello a legend, and the wood-burning oven + Sicilian/NY hybrid menu makes it the strongest pre-bowling pair for The Gutter (200 N 14th St, ~0.7 mi / 4-min drive north). Phone (718) 599-2210. Slices ~$4-5, whole pies ~$22-26. Street parking on Havemeyer/S 1st is doable on weekends but tight; muni lot at Berry & N 7th is a fallback. Order at the counter, eat in or take the box to The Gutter's lounge (they tolerate outside food with drinks). Frank Pinello also operates a second location at 800 Grand St — same menu, easier parking, but the Havemeyer original is the iconic one.

name: Skinny Dennis
desc: Zero-cover Williamsburg honky-tonk with live country nightly, frozen Willie's coffee cocktails, open 'til 4AM
longDesc: NYC's premier honky-tonk bar at 152 Metropolitan Ave (at Berry St), open since Feb 2013 by the Lucky Dog crew. Free live country and roots music every night on a small stage, 18 beers on draft, signature cocktails, vintage jukebox, and the famous Willie's Frozen Coffee. No-frills cash-friendly room with a kitschy Texan-roadhouse feel — pairs naturally with The Gutter (~4 min drive / ~10 min walk) for an active-then-chill Williamsburg evening arc.
notes: Daily 12PM–4AM, no cover charge for live music (skinnydennisbrooklyn.com). Live country/roots music every night since 2013 (Gothamist). Weekend street parking on Metropolitan/Berry/Wythe is plausible but tight; Williamsburg Hotel garage and Wythe Hotel valet are nearby paid backups. 21+, cash + cards. Pairs with The Gutter (200 N 14th St) — 4 min drive or 10 min walk — for the 'active then chill' arc called out in the brief.

name: Brooklyn Steel
desc: 1,800-cap Bowery Presents warehouse venue in Greenpoint hosting indie, rock, and hip-hop tours
longDesc: Brooklyn Steel is a converted East Williamsburg/Greenpoint steel fabrication building turned 1,800-capacity concert hall operated by The Bowery Presents (AEG). It's the largest Bowery-run room in Brooklyn — one tier above Music Hall of Williamsburg — with a main floor, balcony, and three bars; 2026 calendar includes Iron & Wine (May 13), Kevin Morby (June 10), Wolfmother (June 23), Dry Cleaning, The Black Angels, and They Might Be Giants.
notes: 319 Frost St near Debevoise (zip 11222) — East Williamsburg/Greenpoint border (bowerypresents.com). No on-site parking but a lot across the street plus street parking on Frost/Meeker (prked.com). Drive from Industry City via BQE runs ~22-28 min on weekends. Capacity 1,800 with main floor + balcony + three bars (venuereport.com). Phone (888) 929-7849. Bowery Presents 2026 lineup confirmed across Bandsintown, Songkick, and Ticketmaster.

name: Warsaw at the Polish National Home
desc: Punk-rock concert hall where Polish grandmas serve pierogi mid-set — 'pierogi meets punk' since 2001.
longDesc: Housed in a 1914 Polish cultural hall at 261 Driggs Ave in Greenpoint, Warsaw is a 1,100-cap concert room where the in-house Warsaw Bistro slings pierogi, blintzes, kielbasa, and hunters' stew while bands play. A 2023 renovation expanded the balcony, modernized the bars, and improved ADA access without touching the unrepeatable wood-paneled-banquet-hall character. Eat then watch in the same room — there is no other Brooklyn venue that delivers this combination.
hoursWeekend: Show nights only; doors typically 1 hr before set; box office day-of-show
notes: Ticketed shows only — check warsawconcerts.com or Live Nation calendar before planning the night (warsawconcerts.com/visit). Free street parking in Greenpoint is plentiful on weekends; SpotHero pre-books available. Bistro is cash + card after 2023 reno. Capacity ~1,100, GA floor + balcony. Phone (929) 441-3114. Drive from IC is BQE north ~22 min off-peak.

name: Baby's All Right
desc: 280-cap South Williamsburg indie room with restaurant — sub-headliner discovery before bands graduate to Music Hall.
longDesc: Opened 2013 in the former Hygrade Food Products hot-dog factory at 146 Broadway, Baby's All Right is a three-room compound — Live Room, Front Lounge, and Restaurant — that anchors Brooklyn's indie booking pipeline (sub-headliners here often jump to Music Hall of Williamsburg next year). Recent/upcoming May 2026 weekends include Red Rum Club + Ollie Gullick (Fri 5/1), Suzy Sheer + Lea Jaffe (Sat 5/2), Snuggle two-night stand (Mon-Tue 5/4–5/5), Accessory + Golden Apples (Wed 5/6), Antony Szmierek (Sat 5/9 7:30pm), and Nana Grizol (Mon 5/11). Doors usually 6:30–7pm, late sets often added 10:30pm on weekends; you can eat in the front restaurant without a ticket and walk into the show after.
notes: Address 146 Broadway, Brooklyn NY 11211 — base of the Williamsburg Bridge, South Williamsburg side (Wikipedia). 280 standing capacity across three rooms — Live Room, Front Lounge, Restaurant (The Vendry, Wikipedia). Sub-headliner discovery venue — bands often graduate to Music Hall of Williamsburg or Brooklyn Steel within 12–18 months. May 2026 weekend slate from JamBase/Songkick listings: Red Rum Club + Ollie Gullick (Fri 5/1), Suzy Sheer + Lea Jaffe (Sat 5/2), Andrew Lucier (Sun 5/3), Antony Szmierek (Sat 5/9 7:30pm) (JamBase). Full calendar lives on seetickets.us/eventim.us — site auth-walled, so check babysallright.com first then hop to the calendar link. Weekend parking: metered street along Broadway/Bedford is free Sundays, paid Saturday; safer to take Berry St or Driggs side streets and walk 3-4 blocks. Restaurant doesn't require a show ticket — handy if you're early or undecided.

name: Gowanus Gardens
desc: Neighborhood bar with a string-lit rainbow back patio, craft cocktails, and bar-snack kitchen on 4th Ave.
longDesc: Opened by three Gowanus locals at 256 4th Ave, Gowanus Gardens pairs a long indoor bar with a spacious, string-light-covered back patio painted in rainbow stripes — heated and partially covered for shoulder-season hangs. The menu leans playful (fried pickles, pulled pork, Spam musubi) alongside craft beer on tap and quirky cocktails like the Anejo-and-eggnog 'Nog's Yer Druncle.' Late kitchen hours (1a Sun–Thu, 2a Fri–Sat) make it a strong post-IC dinner spot for outdoor drinks.
notes: Outdoor beer-garden-style patio across 4th Ave from the old Mission Dolores footprint — directly fills the 'outdoor drinks near IC' bucket (Gothamist). 21+ after 8pm; no pets. Weekend metered parking on 4th Ave; side-street parking on Carroll/President. Happy hour Mon–Fri 3–7p (gowanusgardensbk.com).

name: Seven Bridges (Permanently Closed)
desc: Closed beer bar in former Mission Dolores space; courtyard now dormant — do not route guests here
longDesc: Seven Bridges opened in spring 2023 in the former Mission Dolores space at 249 4th Ave, run by the team behind The Hop Shop on Columbia St, inheriting the converted auto-body footprint and outdoor courtyard with 2pm–4am daily hours (Patch, BKMAG). Multiple aggregators (Yelp, Foursquare, Untappd) now list the venue as permanently closed as of late 2025, and no successor tenant is publicly announced for the address. Keep flagged as unavailable until a new operator surfaces; the courtyard remains a strong candidate spec for any replacement worth re-researching.
notes: CLOSED — do not surface in itineraries. Seven Bridges (Hop Shop owners) succeeded Mission Dolores ~2023 (Patch, BKMAG 2023-04-26) but is now listed Closed on Yelp/Foursquare/Untappd as of late 2025. Replacement tenant at 249 4th Ave unknown. Re-research trigger: new liquor-license filing or press mention at this address.

name: Brooklyn Game Lab
desc: Park Slope tabletop hangout with weekend Pokemon, Magic, and D&D drop-ins — family-leaning but with adult leagues.
longDesc: Two adjacent storefronts on 7th Ave (479 'Center Slope' and 481 'Annex') stocked with hundreds of board games, RPG kits, and a steady weekend rhythm: Saturday Pokemon Club 2-4pm, Magic: The Gathering League 4-6pm, and Friday/Saturday Night D&D for teens and adults. Core audience is 6-18, but the evening league play and teen passes (Sat 2-6pm at the Annex) make it a credible low-key stop if you want a different intensity register near IC — think families warming up, hobbyists swapping decks, no bar/restaurant noise.
notes: Two storefronts: 479 7th Ave (Center Slope) and 481 7th Ave (Annex), Brooklyn NY 11215 (yelp.com). Saturday afternoons: Pokemon 2-4pm, Magic 4-6pm at Center Slope; Teen Hang 2-6pm at the Annex (hisawyer.com). Friday/Saturday Night D&D listed in site nav (brooklyngamelab.com). Phone 718.788.1122. Mostly kid/teen-oriented programming — adults welcome at league play but this is not a 'board game bar'. 7th Ave metered parking on weekends; side streets (8th/9th/10th) are easier. ~13 min drive from IC up 4th Ave to 9th St.

name: Hex & Co. Union Square
desc: Manhattan board game cafe with 500+ games, full bar, cafe menu, and TCG/RPG event space.
longDesc: Hex & Co.'s Union Square outpost (801 Broadway) is the brand's closest location to Brooklyn — a full bar and cafe wrapped around a 500+ title board game library with pro-run D&D, MTG/Pokemon TCG events, and youth programming. Tabletop play runs $15/player with student discounts Mon–Thu; weekends are heavily booked, so the venue strongly recommends reserving a table online.
notes: Manhattan exception, NOT in Brooklyn — 801 Broadway near Union Square / Greenwich Village; zoned as 'dumbo' because it's the closest enum value (across the Manhattan Bridge). Drive from IC is ~30 min via Gowanus Expy + Manhattan Bridge with no Brooklyn-style street parking — expect to use a paid garage on E 11th/University Pl. $15/player game fee covers unlimited library access (hexnyc.com). Walk-ins welcome but weekend reservations strongly advised due to 'high visitation Sat–Sun' (hexnyc.com). Only justify routing here if a guest specifically wants the Hex brand or pairs it with a Union Square / Strand Bookstore stop; otherwise prefer Brooklyn Strategist (Cobble Hill) or Twenty Sided Store (Williamsburg) for the driving-preferred radius.

name: Marlow & Sons (CLOSED 2025)
desc: Permanently closed in 2025 after 21 years — Andrew Tarlow's seminal South Williamsburg cafe/oyster bar at 81 Broadway.
longDesc: Marlow & Sons opened in 2004 next door to Diner and helped define Brooklyn's farm-to-table era under Andrew Tarlow's Marlow Collective. The Marlow Collective site now lists its run as '2004 – 2025,' and Yelp shows the 81 Broadway location as CLOSED. Do not schedule — kept in the corpus only to block re-discovery and to anchor replacements within the same Broadway micro-cluster around Twenty Sided Store.
notes: CLOSED. The Marlow Collective explicitly lists the dates as '2004 – 2025' (themarlowcollective.com/sons), and Yelp's current listing reads 'MARLOW & SONS - CLOSED - Updated April 2026' (yelp.com). Sister spots Diner (next door) and Roman's are also under the same closure wave — verify before promoting any Tarlow venue. For the Twenty Sided afternoon pairing, route the food stop to one of the enqueued replacements still trading on Broadway/S. 6th.

name: Sip & Play
desc: Park Slope's first board game cafe — 500+ games with boba, beer, wine, and snacks
longDesc: Sip & Play at 471 5th Ave is Park Slope's pioneer board game cafe, stocking over 500 titles from quick party fillers to deep euro strategy. Pay $10/person on weekdays or $12 on Fri-Sun for 3 hours of unlimited gameplay, with a kitchen turning out sandwiches, salads, apps, plus boba tea, beer, and wine. Walk-ins are welcome but Tock reservations guarantee a table on weekends.
notes: $12/person weekends + holidays buys 3 hrs of any of 500+ games (sipnplaynyc.com). Full bar with boba, beer, wine, coffee; kitchen does apps/sandwiches/salads (mommypoppins.com). Reservations via Tock recommended Sat afternoons. Street parking on 5th Ave is feasible but tight — leaves 11min drive back to IC via 4th Ave.

name: Beacon's Closet — Park Slope
desc: Iconic Brooklyn vintage + consignment on Park Slope's 5th Ave shopping strip, same block as Sip & Play
longDesc: Beacon's Closet is the destination Brooklyn vintage/used-clothing store, with this Park Slope outpost at 92 5th Ave sitting in the densest stretch of weekend foot traffic on the avenue. Rotating racks of designer-and-streetwear consignment (women's, men's, accessories) plus a buy/sell/trade counter make it a 30–60 min stop that anchors a stroll between Sip & Play, indie bookstores, and the brunch spots clustered between St Marks and Sterling. Cash + card accepted; gets busy 1–4pm on Saturdays so go earlier or later.
notes: Located at 92 5th Ave between St Marks Pl and Warren St; Sat/Sun 11am–8pm (source: beaconscloset.com locations page). Drive from Industry City via 3rd Ave → Atlantic → 5th Ave is ~12–14 min weekends. Metered street parking on 5th Ave or the Park Slope Municipal Lot at 343 6th Ave (~5 min walk). Pairs naturally with Sip & Play (119 5th Ave) and the dense 5th Ave retail row — Annie's Blue Ribbon General Store, The Ripped Bodice romance bookshop, Bird boutique — for a 2–3 hour Park Slope stroll. Note on original topic: Uncommon Goods at 140 58th St inside Industry City is HQ/fulfillment only with no regular public storefront (source: Wikipedia, Uncommon Goods company entry); occasional sample sales would need date-specific research, not a standing itinerary anchor.

name: Hibino
desc: Kyoto-style obanzai, fresh house-made tofu, and sushi — a 10-min drive from IC and 5 min from Brooklyn Strategist.
longDesc: Tiny Cobble Hill Japanese spot open since 2007, serving daily-changing obanzai small plates ($5 each, written on chalkboards), fresh tofu made in-house, and traditional plus new-style sushi. Perfect early dinner after an afternoon at Brooklyn Strategist — closed Sundays/Wednesdays, no reservations, so arrive at the 4:30 PM open or expect a short wait.
notes: Corner of Henry & Pacific, ~5 min drive from Brooklyn Strategist on Court St. Cash-friendly small room, no reservations — arrive at 4:30 PM open for an early dinner slot. Daily obanzai chalkboard rotates; tonkatsu and house tofu are signatures (theinfatuation.com). Weekend street parking on Pacific or Clinton is usually available; metered on Henry. Pairs well with afternoon gaming since you can hold the table after a board-game session without rushing.

name: LittleMan Parking — 262 S. 4th St. Garage
desc: 24/7 valet garage in South Williamsburg, ~0.2 mi from Grand St — solid fallback when 456 Grand sells out.
longDesc: LittleMan-operated indoor garage at 262 S. 4th Street (between Roebling and Havemeyer), about a 3-minute walk to the Grand St / North Williamsburg dining strip. Open 24/7 with valet service; bookable via ParkWhiz, BestParking, and SpotHero. Use as a backup when the nearby 456 Grand garage shows sold-out weekend inventory.
notes: Valet, indoor, 24/7 access (ParkWhiz). Published reference daily rate ~$16 (BestParking aggregator) but weekend prepay rates on ParkWhiz/SpotHero vary by arrival/departure window — check live booking before relying on a number. Distance to Grand St spine: ~0.2 mi / 4 min walk via S. 4th → Havemeyer → Grand.

name: Greenpoint Weekend Parking Guide (Manhattan Ave / Franklin St)
desc: Where to park free Sunday or for $15-25 Saturday near Greenpoint's main commercial spine.
longDesc: Greenpoint's two-corridor commercial zone — Manhattan Ave (Polish/Eastern European) and Franklin St (newer cafes, galleries, bars) — is reachable by car with predictable parking if you plan around two rules. Sundays: every parking meter in NYC is free (per NYC DOT) and Alternate Side Parking is suspended, so residential side streets like Java, India, Huron, Eagle, and Freeman become open game from late morning. Saturdays: meters run roughly 9:00-19:00 on the commercial blocks themselves, but two blocks east (toward McGolrick Park along Russell, Monitor, Kingsland) or west (toward the waterfront along West St, Franklin's quieter end) usually has free or 1-hour residential parking with the SP+ 27 Eagle St garage ($15-52 day-rate) as a paid backstop.
hoursWeekend: Sat meters 9:00-19:00 / Sun free all day
notes: Practical playbook for arriving from Industry City via BQE (Exit 32A, McGuinness Blvd N): (1) **Sunday is the cheat code** — meters are free citywide and ASP is suspended (nyc.gov/dot), so circle Java/India/Huron/Eagle for a residential spot, no payment, no time limit. (2) **Saturday meters** run on Manhattan Ave + Franklin St themselves (~$1.25-2.00/hr via ParkNYC); they're enforced until 19:00 and turnover is fast around brunch hours (11:00-14:00). (3) **Free-parking corridors that stay open most Saturdays**: Monitor St + Kingsland Ave between Driggs and Nassau (east of Manhattan Ave, near McGolrick Park) often have residential parking with 1-hour daytime caps that lift after 18:00 (spotangels.com). (4) **Garage fallback**: SP+ 27 Eagle St Garage runs $15-52 same-day depending on duration; SP+ 1 Blue Slip Garage by the ferry runs $12-45 (parkmobile.io) — book ahead via SpotHero for 20-30% off rack rate. (5) **Avoid**: McGuinness Blvd shoulder (active tow zone), Franklin St between Greenpoint Ave and Java (commercial loading zones M-Sat 7-19), and anywhere in front of a hydrant (NYC tickets these aggressively, $115). (6) **Coming from IC**: BQE traffic westbound is lightest before 11:00 Saturday and almost any time Sunday — late-afternoon return (16:00-18:00) is the worst slot on either day.

name: NYC Saturday Meter Rules — Brooklyn Cheat Sheet
desc: Saturday meters are ON in Brooklyn — typical 9am–7pm, $1/hr base, no anti-feed, free if a major holiday lands Saturday.
longDesc: Reference card for every Brooklyn stop on a Saturday itinerary. NYC parking meters ARE enforced on Saturdays (not suspended like Sundays). Standard Brooklyn meters run roughly 9am–7pm at $1/hr base; muni-meter and commercial zones in Downtown Brooklyn / DUMBO / Williamsburg can run later and cost more — always read the post. Meters go dark on six legal holidays (New Year's, Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas) even when those fall on a Saturday. Pay via ParkNYC app (zone number printed on the sign) or at the muni-meter with card/coin; you cannot 'feed' the meter past the posted max, and time does not transfer between blocks.
notes: Saturday = paid meter day citywide; only Sundays + 6 major holidays are free (NYC DOT). Brooklyn base rate $1.00/hr, higher in commercial cores like Downtown Brooklyn and DUMBO (NYC DOT parking-rates). 'Anti-feeding' is enforced — buy the posted max, then move the car to a different block if you need more time (NYC 311). ParkNYC app supports pay-ahead up to 1 hour before regs begin; zone number is on the post (NYC 311). Commercial-vehicle-only restrictions are Mon–Fri 7am–6pm, so passenger cars can usually use those signed spots on Saturday (NYC DOT commercial-vehicle parking) — still read the sign for muni-meter overlay. SpotAngels and the State Assembly 2026 parking calendar are useful for holiday-by-holiday lookup but treat them as secondary to nyc.gov.

name: JTunes Karaoke Bar
desc: 10 private karaoke rooms inside Japan Village at IC — order ramen/sushi straight to your room.
longDesc: Brooklyn's newest karaoke bar opened inside Japan Village at Industry City Building 4, with 10 private rooms holding parties of 1-12 and a walk-up bar where singing is also welcome. A QR code at the table lets you order from all the Japan Village courtyard vendors (ramen, sushi, takoyaki) and have it delivered to your room while you sing, paired with signature Japanese cocktails. Deposit required to book; weekend-only operations (Thu-Sun) make late Saturday slots the sweet spot for after-dinner sessions.
notes: On-site at IC Building 4 (220 36th St) inside the Japan Village courtyard — zero drive from a Sake's Bar dinner stop (source: industrycity.com/tenants/j-tunes). 10 private rooms, party size 1-12, deposit required to book; large parties (10+) need 3-day catering notice (source: toast.app/r/jtunes). No outside food/drink — order via in-room QR from Japan Village vendors. Book ahead for weekend nights: (917) 679-5983 or JTunes@japanvillage.com. Closed Mon-Wed.

name: Kuraichi
desc: NYC's deepest Japanese sake, shochu, awamori & whisky shop tucked inside Japan Village.
longDesc: Kuraichi is the liquor wing of Japan Village in Industry City (Building 4, 88 35th St), stocking hundreds of sakes organized by genre — dry, fruity, umami, smooth — alongside junmai/ginjo/nigori/nama types, plus Japanese whisky with assorted cask finishes, shochu and awamori. Staff picks rotate monthly with discounts, and they run tastings and special-order service. A perfect quick pickup paired with a Japan Village food-hall lap before heading to a drinks stop.
notes: Inside Japan Village at IC Building 4 (industrycity.com). Bottles roughly $26-$48+ with premium options higher (kuraichibk.com). Pair with Japan Village food stalls then drive to a drinks venue; ask staff for a 'staff pick' for a curated tasting at home. Tel (646) 460-3765.

name: Le Crocodile
desc: All-day French brasserie inside the Wythe Hotel with a kitchen that runs to 11pm on weekends.
longDesc: Le Crocodile is the Williamsburg brasserie from Chez Ma Tante chefs Aidan O'Neal and Jake Leiber, tucked into the lobby of the Wythe Hotel at 80 Wythe Ave. It serves earnest French fare — steak frites, escargot, roast chicken — in a Parisian-meets-NY room, and the kitchen stays open until 11pm Thursday through Saturday, making it a reliable late-dinner fallback when Greenpoint spots like Midnights wind down early.
notes: Located in Wythe Hotel lobby, 80 Wythe Ave, Williamsburg (lecrocodile.com). Hours: Mon-Wed & Sun 7am-10pm, Thu-Sat 7am-11pm — one of the later kitchens in north Brooklyn (yelp.com, nyctourism.com). Reservations via Resy strongly recommended for weekend dinner; walk-ins more feasible at the bar. Hotel valet plus paid street parking on Wythe/N 11th; weekend curbside is tight but doable past 9pm. Strong fallback when Greenpoint late-night spots close early; pairs well with a Bar Blondeau rooftop nightcap upstairs at the Wythe.

name: Chez Moi
desc: Cozy Atlantic Ave French bistro — steak frites, escargot, absinthe bar, weekend brunch to late dinner.
longDesc: A romantic, bookshelf-lined French bistro on Atlantic Ave at the Brooklyn Heights/Cobble Hill border, doing classic bouillabaisse, côte de boeuf, escargots, oysters and profiteroles alongside a notable absinthe selection. Opens 10am for weekend brunch (croque madame, frittatas) and runs straight through to 11:30pm dinner service, so it slots into either a late-lunch or post-sunset itinerary slot. Side-street parking on Henry/Hicks/State is materially easier than the Smith St corridor in Carroll Gardens.
notes: 135 Atlantic Ave, sits on the Heights/Cobble Hill line (Tripadvisor lists Cobble Hill, the restaurant's own site says Brooklyn Heights). Drive from IC via Hamilton Ave → BQE → Atlantic Ave exit, ~15 min off-peak. Parking advantage vs Carroll Gardens French alternatives: Atlantic Ave meters are free Sundays and after 7pm Sat, and the Heights side streets (Henry, Hicks, State, Pacific) turn over more reliably than Smith St's permit-heavy residential blocks (chezmoiny.com; nyc.gov DOT meter rules). Reservations via Resy recommended for Sat dinner.

name: Bacchus Bistro & Wine Bar
desc: Bordeaux-native-owned French bistro on Atlantic Ave with a hidden back garden and 25+ wines by the glass
longDesc: Boerum Hill institution opened in 2003 by Bordeaux native Bruno Laclide, pouring wines from every major French region — organic, biodynamic, and a 'cave cachée' of rare bottles (Petrus, Yquem). The intimate dining room opens onto a leafy back garden seating, and the rotating six-app/six-entrée menu runs classics like French onion soup, mussels, foie gras, and braised lamb shank. About 10 minutes by car from Industry City via the Gowanus Expressway.
notes: Owner Bruno Laclide is Bordeaux-born; wine bar wing added summer 2015 with 25+ by-the-glass pours (bacchusbistro.com/about). Back garden open for dinner 7 nights/week and used for private events (bacchusbistro.com). Yelp shows 610 reviews as of May 2026 confirming active operation; an older Yelp duplicate is incorrectly marked CLOSED — verify by the live OpenTable page (opentable.com/bacchus-brooklyn). Weekend street parking on Atlantic/Bond is realistic; metered lots on Pacific St. Vegetarian-friendly via apps, salads, and rotating veg entrée — not a vegan or gluten-free destination.

name: Zimmi's
desc: Intimate 37-seat Provençal bistro in West Village (Manhattan) — regional South-of-France country cooking, opened Dec 2024.
longDesc: Chef Maxime Pradié — a New Yorker who spent childhood summers with his grandmother in Provence — channels rustic Southern French cooking at this corner spot on Bedford Street: pissaladière niçoise, lamb stew (agneau), pasta davia with basil pesto, sage chicken ragout, asparagus two ways (truffle sabayon + hazelnut vinaigrette). Owner Jenni Guizio (former wine/beverage director for Danny Meyer's Union Square Hospitality Group) shaped the wine list and the unpretentious countryside-inn design: brown-and-white checked tablecloths, wooden banquettes, sheer half-curtains, softly glowing sconces. Uniquely justifies the Manhattan trip because it fills a regional-French gap (Provence-heritage, not generic Parisian bistro) left by La Cigogne and is a fresh, currently-operating venue.
notes: ACTUAL LOCATION: 72 Bedford St, New York, NY 10014 — West Village, Manhattan (not Brooklyn). Drive from Industry City via Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel ~20-25 min weekend daytime, can stretch to 30+ Sat night. Weekend parking is the catch: no garage on-site and West Village street parking is brutal on Fri/Sat evenings — closest paid lots are Pier 40 (West & Houston) and Charlton St garage, both ~5-min walk. Reservations strongly recommended (only 37 seats). Per The Taste Bud (Apr 2025), plates run $16-$45; foie-gras starters and lamb mains push the check upward (source: Taste Bud Substack, Business-Style review, Fine Dining Lovers). Signature dishes per coverage: pissaladière, agneau/lamb stew, pasta davia with basil pesto, asparagus two ways, triple vanilla ice cream with brown-butter shortbread. Hours: nightly dinner only, no lunch service. Wine list leans natural/Old World per Jenni Guizio's USHG pedigree (source: Exhibit A, OpenTable blog).

name: Maison Provence
desc: South-of-France bistro in Williamsburg with Niçois chef, ratatouille, and Monday French Connection nights
longDesc: A regional, rustic Williamsburg bistro inspired by the Côte d'Azur and run by Nice-born Chef Lolo — the menu leans Provençal (ratatouille, charcuterie boards, savory crepes, duck breast fettuccine) rather than the standard Paris-bistro template. Mondays bring 'French Connection Night' with 20% off select wines, live French music and French-speaking staff; Thursdays 4–6 PM host an outdoor Paint & Sip. The Havemeyer Street location sits in residential Williamsburg with mostly metered weekend street parking nearby.
notes: 52 Havemeyer St, Williamsburg (maisonprovencebk.com). Chef Lolo from Nice — explicitly southern-France focus, not Paris-default (brooklyndowntownstar.com 2025-05-27). Signature: ratatouille (vegetarian), Provençal crepes, duck breast fettuccine, rustic charcuterie (Yelp). Weekend hours Fri–Sun 11:00–22:30 (official site). Resy reservations available. Monday French Connection Night 5:00–22:30 with 20% off wines, live music — worth noting for non-weekend planning. Outdoor Paint & Sip Thursdays 4–6 PM. Parking: metered street parking on Havemeyer/S. 4th–5th, easier before 18:00 on Saturdays.

name: Mr. Bing (Industry City) — Permanently Closed
desc: Beijing-style jianbing stall once inside Japan Village; chain shuttered after Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2024.
longDesc: Mr. Bing was a small NYC chain selling Beijing-style jianbing (savory crepes with egg, hoisin, chili, scallion, and crisp wonton). Owner Brian Goldberg filed Chapter 7 in June 2024 and liquidated all six units, including any Industry City / Japan Village presence (Restaurant Hospitality, 2024). The packaged chili crisp brand (mr-bing.com) survives, but no storefront remains; Yelp listings for every NYC location are tagged CLOSED through 2025-2026. Do not route foodie tracks here.
notes: DO NOT PROMOTE. Chain bankrupt June 2024, all six NYC units liquidated (Restaurant Hospitality). Yelp confirms all locations CLOSED through 2026. Brand survives only as packaged chili crisp at mr-bing.com. Use enqueued substitutes to fulfill the Sunrise Mart shopping+lunch loop instead — Japan Village Food Hall itself is the natural pivot since it sits inside the same Building 3/4 complex (934 3rd Ave) and is open Fri-Sat 11:00-20:30, Sun 11:00-19:00.

name: Japan Village Snack Flight (Sunrise Mart + Food Hall)
desc: DIY konbini-style tasting flight: build a snack tray at Sunrise Mart, eat in the food hall.
longDesc: Inside Industry City Building B, Japan Village pairs the largest Japanese grocery store in NYC (Sunrise Mart) with an 11-stall food hall under one roof. Build a Family Mart-style tasting flight by grabbing 6-8 items off the snack wall (Calbee jagariko, Pocky variants, melon pan, onigiri, Pocari Sweat, mochi ice cream, Black Thunder bars, seasonal Kit Kats) plus a hot bite from a stall (takoyaki, okonomiyaki, or curry pan), then assemble at a communal table. Spending $50+ at Sunrise Mart validates 2 hours of parking in the Industry City lot.
notes: Anchor venue at IC Building B, 934 3rd Ave — same address houses Sunrise Mart and the food hall stalls (Yelp, japanvillage.com). Snack-flight angle: pick one of each Family Mart category (savory chip, sweet biscuit, gummy/jelly, onigiri/rice item, hot pastry, bottled drink, ice cream) for a structured tasting. Hit Sunrise Mart first for cold/shelf items, then add a hot stall item (Wakuwaku izakaya for sit-down, or grab-and-go from the food hall counters). Validated parking in IC lot with $50+ Sunrise Mart spend, 2hr cap (japanvillage.com/directions). Weekend street parking around IC buildings is largely open. Vegetarian-friendly snack wall; halal/gluten-free options limited — check labels (many Japanese snacks contain pork gelatin or wheat).

name: Tikuran Ramen
desc: Compact standalone ramen-ya in Sunset Park — Tokyo tonkotsu shoyu and miso bowls, broth-first, no food-hall chaos.
longDesc: A small Sunset Park ramen shop (~8 min south of IC) focused on rich broths and springy noodles rather than a sprawling menu. Tokyo Tonkotsu Shoyu with extra chashu and the miso ramen with corn + egg are the picks; karaage and a few buns round it out. Quiet, casual, counter-friendly — the antidote to a packed Japan Village on Sunrise Mart days.
notes: 732 61st St, Sunset Park — standalone shop, not the food hall (ZipPicks). ~1.8 mi south of IC via 3rd Ave → 7th Ave. Street parking, manageable with a few blocks of circling, tougher after 6pm (ZipPicks). Weekend wait ~15-25 min at peak; shorter solo at counter. Pairs naturally with a Sunrise Mart grocery run — drive over after shopping if Japan Village is slammed. Note: Ramen Setagaya at 934 3rd Ave is *inside* Japan Village/IC, so it's not a viable overflow option (Tripadvisor).

name: Ramen Setagaya (Japan Village)
desc: Tokyo-style shio ramen counter inside Japan Village food hall at Industry City Building 4.
longDesc: Setagaya runs a stall inside Japan Village, NYC's first Japanese food hall, in IC Building 4 at 934 3rd Ave. The signature is a delicate shio (salt) broth built from dried fish, kelp and chicken; the showpiece Mt. Fuji bowl piles grated parmesan over a chili-tomato-rimmed tonkotsu. Counter seating in the hall, easy walk to Sunrise Mart grocery, Hachi (okonomiyaki), Gohei (soba/udon) and the Wakuwaku izakaya — making it a self-contained rainy-day cluster.
notes: Located at 934 3rd Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11232 inside Japan Village food hall in IC Building 4 (yelp.com/biz/japan-village-brooklyn). Stall hours Mon-Thu & Sun 11:30-19:30, Fri-Sat 11:30-20:30 (setagayany.com); surrounding hall stays open until 21:00 on Fri-Sat. Founded by Tsukasa Maejima (NYC since 2007). Real ramen anchor — replaces the previous incorrect 'Mokbar at IC' reference (Mokbar is at Chelsea Market, Manhattan). Pairs naturally with Sunrise Mart browsing, Hachi or Wakuwaku for a multi-stop Japan Village loop without leaving the building.

name: D-Jing K Korean Kitchen
desc: Chef Joy's fast-casual Korean stall inside Industry City Food Hall — bibimbap, spicy noodles, Korean wings, banchan.
longDesc: D-Jing is Chef Joy's first dedicated Korean concept, tucked into the Industry City Food Hall in Building 2 with 'Seoulful street eats' done right — bibimbap bowls, spicy noodles, bulgogi, mandu dumplings, Korean wings and a rotating banchan lineup. Bold, comforting flavors at food-hall speed, which makes it the actual on-campus Korean comfort stop (filling the role the itinerary previously imagined Mokbar would). Order at counter, eat at communal tables, then drift to the surrounding stalls and the IC courtyard.
notes: Inside IC Food Hall, Building 2, entrance at 238 36th St (industrycity.com). Weekend hours Fri-Sun 11am-8pm; weekday close is 7:30pm. Fast-casual counter service — pair with a bao or coffee from neighboring stalls. Bibimbap and Korean wings are the signature orders; mandu and tom yum-style noodles round out the menu (djingkfood.nyc). IC parking lot makes this trivial when you're already on campus.

name: Ms. Yoo
desc: Esther Choi's LES Korean-American gastropub — playful bar food + cocktails, the inverse of Mokbar.
longDesc: Bi-level 50-seat Korean-American gastropub on Allen Street, named for chef Esther Choi's grandmother Jungok Yoo. Where Mokbar serves authentic Korean with American accents, Ms. Yoo flips the equation — American bar favorites rebuilt with Korean technique (Tteok n' Cheese with rice cakes + gruyère, bone marrow with kimchi onion jam, soju-forward cocktail program). Opens at 5 PM, so it slots cleanly as a Manhattan date-night finisher after a Brooklyn afternoon track.
notes: Manhattan venue — included as date-night sibling to Mokbar in the Esther Choi family (FSR magazine). Address 163 Allen St, LES; opens daily from 5 PM (BroadwayWorld preview). Weekend parking is tough on Allen — recommend Icon garage at Houston/Suffolk or Delancey-Essex Municipal lot. IC → Williamsburg Bridge → Allen St is the cleanest driving route. Pair with a return drink in Williamsburg before crossing back to IC. Not for kid-track itineraries; cocktails-forward.

name: Oldies
desc: Intimate 12-seat Japanese cocktail bar adjacent to WakuWaku — fresh-fruit cocktails, Toki highballs, City Pop on vinyl.
longDesc: From the WakuWaku team at Japan Village, Oldies is a casual old-school Japanese cocktail lounge specializing in spirit-forward drinks, freshly-squeezed fruit cocktails, and highballs with a twist. The 12-seat room runs Tokyo City Pop, Disco, Funk, and New Wave on the soundsystem, with fun bar snacks from the kitchen until ~9:15 PM. Natural post-dinner extension if you're already eating at WakuWaku or Japan Village.
notes: 269 36th St, inside Industry City's Japan Village complex — same address as WakuWaku (wakuwakuny.com). 12-seat lounge per Yelp (yelp.com/biz/oldies-brooklyn-2). Kitchen closes ~45min before bar close. Closed Mon–Tue. Parking on-site at IC garage. Cash-light; reservations via website recommended on Saturdays.

name: Bandai Namco Cross Store Brooklyn
desc: First US flagship of Bandai Namco — Gashapon, Gundam, One Piece, Tamagotchi, Pac-Man inside Japan Village
longDesc: Opened Feb 28, 2025 in Industry City's Japan Village, this is the first US Bandai Namco Cross Store — ten official shops under one roof spanning Gashapon Bandai capsule machines from Japan, BANDAI SPIRITS Gundam model kits, MegaHouse figures, the One Piece Card Game shop, Tamagotchi Shop and PAC-MAN SELECT. An experiential retail venue where fans can see, touch and play with character merch shipped straight from Japan — a genuinely rare US-mainland Bandai Namco footprint, not just a pop-up.
notes: Inside Industry City Building 4, Japan Village, 2F — anchor address 52 35th St (Industry City complex also listed as 220 36th St / Building 4) (industrycity.com). Free on-site IC parking on weekends. Pair with Japan Village food hall downstairs for an easy anime-fan combo. Instagram @bncrossstore_us. Anime News Network confirms US-first flagship status (animenewsnetwork.com).

name: Llama Inn (Permanently Closed Dec 2025)
desc: Former higher-end Peruvian on Withers St in Williamsburg; closed Dec 2025 after ~10 years — not bookable.
longDesc: Llama Inn was Erik Ramirez's acclaimed modern Peruvian restaurant at 50 Withers St in Williamsburg. After about a decade of service it closed permanently in late December 2025 (Greenpointers, 2025-12-03; Yelp and OpenTable now list it as closed as of 2026). Retained here only to prevent re-queueing; do not include in active itineraries — see enqueued Williamsburg replacements for higher-end dinner anchors.
notes: PERMANENTLY CLOSED — Llama Inn shuttered late December 2025 after ten years at 50 Withers St (Greenpointers 2025-12-03). Yelp and OpenTable confirm closure as of May 2026. Do NOT promote to corpus/itinerary. Original concept was chef Erik Ramirez's modern Peruvian; sister restaurant Llama San in Manhattan is unrelated to the Williamsburg post-show/pre-bowl driving-cluster use case (subway-only Greenwich Village). Replace with another Williamsburg/Greenpoint higher-end dinner — see enqueue.

name: Union Pool
desc: Iconic Williamsburg dive with a huge patio, El Diablo taco truck, and nightly resident DJs 8pm–4am.
longDesc: Union Pool is a 150-cap Williamsburg institution at 484 Union Ave with a former pool-supply storefront converted into a main bar, back room music venue, and a sprawling stone patio with a fountain pond. El Diablo Taco Truck slings late-night Mexican from the yard most nights, and resident DJs spin a wide range 7 nights a week from 8pm–4am — perfect dinner-and-dance plug-in after an IC-anchored cluster night.
notes: Backyard with stone patio + fountain pond open year-round; El Diablo Tacos in the yard most nights (union-pool.com). Resident DJs nightly 8pm–4am (yelp.com). No reservations, no cover for most patio/bar nights — ticketed shows in back room. Street parking in Williamsburg gets tight after 9pm; Lorimer St garage is the safer drop after IC.

name: Spare Room at The Gutter
desc: 1,000 sqft private back room at Williamsburg's vintage bowling bar — BYO DJ, stocked bar, hidden behind the bathrooms
longDesc: Tucked behind the lanes at The Gutter Williamsburg, the Spare Room is a roughly 1,000 sqft private event space with its own bar, stage, and turntables/digital dock for guests to spin their own sets (bandnada.com). It hosts live music, comedy, and karaoke on public nights but flips to private buyouts for birthdays, bachelor/ette parties, and group hangs, with the option to add lanes in the main bowling room ($35/half hr per lane on weekends, per gutterbarbowl.com). The 'secret show room behind the bathrooms' framing makes it a great photo + chill anchor for a North Williamsburg track, especially paired with nearby food and drinks within a few blocks.
notes: 200 N 14th St, Brooklyn NY 11211; 21+ at all times (gutterbarbowl.com/williamsburg). Spare Room is the private buyout space behind the lanes — fully stocked bar, BYO DJ on turntables/digital, stage for live sets (bandnada.com/b/gutterspareroom). Best for group bookings of ~30-80; pair with vintage bowling next door for a single-stop track. Weekend parking is street-only and competitive — recommend rideshare for groups or arriving by 5pm on Saturday. Contact: 718-387-3585.

name: Union Pool
desc: Williamsburg dive with a big back patio, fountain, El Diablo taco truck, and DJs nightly until 4am.
longDesc: A long-running Williamsburg institution housed in a former pool-supply store, Union Pool's main draw is a sprawling fenced back patio with picnic tables, a stone fountain, and the El Diablo taco truck parked in the corner slinging cheap, well-spiced tacos until 3:30-4am. Resident DJs spin seven nights a week, and on summer Saturdays it hosts free outdoor concerts starting at 4pm. Strong fit as a pre/post-show anchor for a Music Hall of Williamsburg night — it's a 7-minute walk away and the patio absorbs a big group without a reservation.
notes: 484 Union Ave, Brooklyn 11211, ~7 min walk to Music Hall of Williamsburg. Back patio open year-round (heated in winter). El Diablo Taco Truck on-site Sat-Sun 13:00-04:00 (Yelp). DJs every night 10pm-4am (NYC Tourism). Free outdoor concerts every Saturday at 4pm in summer (Brooklyn Vegan). Street parking on Union/Meeker is doable on weekend evenings but tight — McCarren Park lots are the nearest backup. Cash-friendly, no cover most nights.

name: Elsewhere
desc: Three-story Bushwick music venue and arts space with a 500-cap rooftop for underground sets and screenings.
longDesc: Elsewhere is a multi-room music venue, nightclub and arts space at 599 Johnson Ave in Bushwick, with five distinct rooms — Zone One (675-cap main), The Hall (~200-cap), Chatroom, The Loft lounge, and a 500-capacity Rooftop that runs DJ sets, parties, and film screenings in warm months. Programming leans 'underground and unbound' — left-field electronic, indie, and experimental — making it a quieter, music-first counterpart to House of Yes within the same Bushwick cluster (timeout.com, brooklynvegan.com).
hoursWeekend: Event-dependent; rooftop typically Fri-Sun afternoons/evenings in season — check calendar
notes: Five rooms incl. Zone One (675), The Hall (200), Chatroom, The Loft, and The Rooftop (500-cap, seasonal) (elsewhere.club). Located at 599 Johnson Ave, Brooklyn 11237; street parking + lots in industrial Bushwick are easier than Williamsburg on weekends. Rooftop debuted Memorial Day weekend with DJ programming and food/drinks (amny.com, timeout.com). ~20 min drive from Industry City via BQE.

name: Westlight
desc: 22nd-floor 360° rooftop cocktail bar atop The William Vale with Manhattan skyline views
longDesc: Perched on the 22nd floor of The William Vale hotel in north Williamsburg, Westlight is Andrew Carmellini's NoHo Hospitality rooftop bar offering 360-degree views of Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the East River. The menu pairs original and classic cocktails with rare spirits, craft beer, wine, and globally inspired small plates. Weekends open at 12pm (21+ after 6pm), and valet parking on-site makes it easy for a pre-Brooklyn-Bowl stop.
notes: Solid Bar Blondeau alternative — 22nd-floor 360° views vs. Blondeau's mid-rise vantage; reservations encouraged on weekends via SevenRooms (westlightnyc.com/reservations). 21+ after 6pm — guests under 21 admitted only before 6pm. Valet parking on-site at The William Vale (NoHo Hospitality / Andrew Carmellini). ~22 min drive from Industry City via BQE; ~7 min north of Brooklyn Bowl Williamsburg, making it a natural pre-show cocktail stop. Address: 111 N 12th St, 22nd Fl, Brooklyn, NY 11249.

name: The Ides at Wythe Hotel (Closed — now Bar Blondeau)
desc: Former 6th-floor Wythe rooftop cocktail bar; closed 2020 and replaced by Bar Blondeau in 2021.
longDesc: The Ides was the original rooftop cocktail-and-views bar on the 6th floor of Wythe Hotel in Williamsburg, known for brass-and-marble interiors, an outdoor terrace facing the Manhattan skyline, and a seasonal cocktail-only program (no food beyond bar snacks). It shuttered during the 2020 hotel pause and was reconceived by the same Andrew Tarlow group as Bar Blondeau, which reopened the space in 2021 with a French small-plates menu, natural wine list, and the same skyline view. Yelp still lists The Ides as 'CLOSED' as of February 2026.
notes: Do not route itineraries here — venue is defunct. Same physical rooftop now operates as Bar Blondeau (already in corpus) which added a food program, so the 'cocktail-only/no-food' contrast point against Bar Blondeau no longer exists at this address. For a true cocktail-only Williamsburg rooftop contrast, see enqueue (Westlight at The William Vale is the strongest like-for-like substitute). Yelp marks 'CLOSED - Updated February 2026' (https://www.yelp.com/biz/the-ides-bar-brooklyn). Wythe Hotel dining page now lists only Bar Blondeau and Le Crocodile, with no mention of The Ides (https://www.wythehotel.com/dining).

name: Bar Blondeau (formerly Lemon's, Wythe Hotel rooftop)
desc: 6th-floor Wythe Hotel rooftop with Manhattan skyline views — 5-min walk from Brooklyn Bowl
longDesc: Bar Blondeau is the rooftop bar on the 6th floor of the Wythe Hotel at 80 Wythe Ave — the same address that was Lemon's (coastal-Italian tiki-leaning concept) from 2019 until it rebranded in 2021. It now runs a seasonal New York cocktail program with East Coast oysters, spicy tuna toast, fried chicken, and steak au poivre, with full-frontal Manhattan skyline views. Weekend hours open early (Sat 2pm, Sun 1pm) making it a strong pre-Brooklyn-Bowl drinks stop just one block from the venue.
notes: NOTE: The task topic 'Lemon's rooftop at Hoxton Williamsburg' is factually incorrect on two counts. (1) Lemon's was at the Wythe Hotel, not the Hoxton (nyctourism.com, afar.com). (2) Lemon's closed and was rebranded as Bar Blondeau in 2021; Yelp lists Lemon's as permanently closed as of Dec 2025 (yelp.com). The Hoxton Williamsburg's actual rooftop is Laser Wolf (thehoxton.com). Bar Blondeau is the substantive, currently-operating successor at 80 Wythe Ave — 5-min walk to Brooklyn Bowl (61 Wythe Ave). Reservations via barblondeau.com or 718-460-8006. Weekend street parking in Williamsburg is tight on show nights; Hoxton/Wythe paid lots nearby.

name: The Keep
desc: Cabinet-of-curiosities cocktail bar on the Bushwick/Ridgewood border with live jazz
longDesc: A dimly lit, antique-festooned drinking room built by Diego and Stephanie Castillo, packed with taxidermy, vintage mirrors, tapestries, armor, weapons, chandeliers and 30 years of curios sourced from Delhi to Peru. Cocktails run $9-$12, well drinks $6, and there's a beer-and-shot special at $5, with small plates like mini-meatballs, kielbasa coins and a vegetarian Mediterranean plate. Live jazz on Wednesdays plus DJs and projection mapping on weekends — it was one of the first bars in the area to program jazz seriously.
notes: Not a Japanese listening bar despite the original research brief — actual concept is antique curio cabinet + cocktails + live jazz, on the Cypress/Starr corner just over the Bushwick/Ridgewood line in Queens (gothamist.com, bushwickdaily.com). Live music Wednesdays from open; weekends feature DJs and projection mapping per the venue (thekeepny.com via we-heart.com). Cocktail prices $9-$12, well drinks $6, beers $6-$7, beer-and-shot $5 (gothamist.com). Open daily 4pm-4am (p2bars.com). Drive from Industry City via BQE/Metropolitan Ave is ~20-25 min off-peak; street parking on Cypress/Starr is generally available evenings. Pairs better with a Bushwick-cluster itinerary (Mood Ring, Birdy's, House of Yes) than with the Kissa Kissa/Japanese-audiophile cluster the original brief assumed.

name: Nako
desc: Sleek Brooklyn Heights cafe with ceremonial-grade matcha soft-serve and balanced matcha lattes
longDesc: Nako is a minimal, design-forward coffee + matcha bar tucked on a quiet block between Brooklyn Heights and Brooklyn Bridge Park. Its matcha program — bold lattes, iced shaken matcha, and a signature soft-serve — has made it one of Brooklyn's go-to modern matcha destinations. Substitute pick because the requested 'Matcha Cafe Maiko at Japan Village' does not exist (Maiko has no Brooklyn location; Japan Village's matcha is served by Panya).
notes: IMPORTANT SUBSTITUTION: The originating queue topic 'Matcha Cafe Maiko at Japan Village' is based on an incorrect premise — Matcha Cafe Maiko has no Brooklyn location (closest is 132 Bowery, Manhattan, ~25 min weekend drive from IC) and Japan Village's matcha vendor is Panya Bakery (matchacafe-maiko.com/eng/store). Nako is the strongest IC-adjacent Brooklyn replacement that hits the same 'matcha soft-serve + lattes' brief and pairs cleanly with a Brooklyn Heights / Brooklyn Bridge Park stop after an IC anchor. Located 18 Columbia Pl between Joralemon St and Atlantic Ave; street parking is generally available on weekends in this residential pocket of Brooklyn Heights (nako.coffee, visitbrooklyn.nyc).

name: Shokusaido at Japan Village
desc: Tempura and kushi-ten counter inside Japan Village food hall — fried-to-order vegetable tempura ~$1/piece
longDesc: Shokusaido is Japan Village's deep-fry specialist, turning out kushi-ten (Japanese deep-fried skewers), karaage-ten, katsu-ten and vegetable tempura made to order. Chefs grind their own bread crumbs in-house and fry pieces as you wait, so timing is everything — order the vegetable assortment hot and eat at the food hall's communal tables. Pairs well as a tempura-focused lunch slot at Industry City when Setagaya ramen is not the goal.
notes: Located inside Japan Village food hall, 934 3rd Ave, Sunset Park — same building as Industry City so 0 min drive (source: japanvillage.com). Specialty is kushi-ten / deep-fried skewers plus vegetable tempura at ~$1/piece, fried to order (source: yelp + tripadvisor reviews). Weekend hours Fri-Sat 12:00-20:30, Sun 12:00-19:30. NOTE: queue topic asked for 'Hatakeyama tempura counter' but no vendor by that name exists at Japan Village — Shokusaido is the actual tempura specialist on the current roster (verified against japanvillage.com/eat-drink, May 2026). If a 'Hatakeyama' stall opens later this should be re-researched.

name: Waku Waku (Japan Village)
desc: Traditional sit-down izakaya inside Japan Village at Industry City — yakitori, kushiage, chuhai, sake flights.
longDesc: Waku Waku is the full-service izakaya tucked into Japan Village's Building 3 at Industry City, run by the same team as the adjacent Oldies sake/cocktail bar. Expect a yakitori-and-kushiage-driven menu with a deep sake list, chuhai cocktails, and Teishoku sets at lunch; the dining room has counter, bar, private rooms, and an outdoor patio. Yakitori skewers skew premium but reviewers consistently call out the negima and kabocha as standouts, with a chill family-friendly room that transitions into a louder evening izakaya vibe.
notes: NOTE: Original topic 'Yopparai NYC at Japan Village' was a misidentification — Yopparai is at 49 Clinton St, LES Manhattan (yopparainyc.com), and has no Industry City location. The sit-down izakaya/sake bar *inside* Japan Village hall is Waku Waku, with sister bar Oldies next door for a drinks-only pivot (industrycity.com tenant page). Closed Mon-Tue. Weekend service runs continuously Sat (no break) and Sun until 20:30 — ideal evening slot after a Mt. Fuji ramen lunch elsewhere in the hall. Reservations recommended weekends; service can lag at peak (multiple Yelp reviews). Yakitori higher-priced but vegetarian skewers (kabocha, shishito) available.

name: Ramen Setagaya (Williamsburg Flagship)
desc: Williamsburg flagship of NYC's niboshi-leaning shio specialist — dried-fish + kelp + chicken broth
longDesc: The Bedford Ave flagship of Tsukasa Maejima's Setagaya (Tokyo, 2000), and the Williamsburg-cluster counterpart to the Industry City branch. Its shio broth is built from niboshi (dried sardines), kelp, and chicken — the closest current expression in NYC of the niboshi-shio bowl Setagaya's original East Village shop was known for before closing in 2017. Counter-style room, 12pm open daily, weekend service into the late evening.
notes: Order the shio for the niboshi-forward bowl — official site describes shio as 'dried fish, kelp, and chicken' (setagayany.com). Regulars also flag the black garlic and spicy miso as standouts (Yelp, 335 reviews / 4.4★ via Google). Bedford Ave parking is tight on weekends; Wythe/N. 7th side streets are easier. Use this card when itinerary already routes through Williamsburg/Greenpoint — otherwise prefer the Industry City Setagaya card for IC-anchored plans.

name: Hana Makgeolli
desc: Only US makgeolli brewery — Korean rice-wine bottle shop, tasting flights, and anju snacks in Greenpoint
longDesc: Alice Jun's Greenpoint brewery is the only operation in the United States producing traditional Korean makgeolli, soju, and cheongju on-site, with a tasting room out front pouring flights alongside anju like pajeon and kimchi arancini. The retail counter sells bottles to take home — traditional, botanical, alternative-grain, and the new 20% ABV Hana Soju — making it the Korean counterpart to Industry City's Japanese sake stops. Optional 45-minute brewery tours Thursday-Sunday end in a guided three-pour tasting.
notes: 201 Dupont St, Brooklyn NY 11222. Friday open 17:00-23:00; brewery tours Thu-Sun by reservation (Resy). Take-home bottles ship nationwide except AL/AR/CT/DE/MI/MS/RI/SD/UT/VA; free NYC local delivery and free shipping over $100 (hanamakgeolli.com/shop). Founded 2017 by Alice Jun, only US makgeolli brewery (Resy, 2024). Drive ~22 min from IC via Gowanus + BQE; Dupont St has weekend street parking. Originally queued as 'Hidden Lee' — that exact venue could not be verified across three web searches, so this is the strongest real fit for the same corpus slot (Korean take-home-bottle adjacent to Kuraichi).

name: UnD
desc: Japan/NY concept café serving ceremonial-grade Uji matcha whisked traditionally, plus shokupan bakery
longDesc: UnD is a Tokyo/New York concept brand that soft-opened in Greenpoint in October 2024 at 141 India St, sourcing ceremonial-grade Uji matcha directly from Kyoto and preparing it with a chagama iron kettle and chasen bamboo whisk. The space pairs the matcha bar with a Japanese bakery program — handmade shokupan, melon bread, wagashi — and a curated tea + matcha retail counter. It's the most authentic ceremonial-grade matcha alternative to Industry City's cafés on the north Brooklyn waterfront.
notes: Ceremonial-grade Uji matcha from Kyoto, whisked with chasen and brewed with a chagama iron kettle for traditional preparation (und-ny.com). Soft-opened October 2024 at 141 India St with Japanese sandwiches, shokupan, wagashi, and a tea/matcha retail wall (Greenpointers). Weekend hours close at 3pm Sat-Sun (vs. 5pm weekdays) — better as a morning anchor than afternoon stop. 20g cans of authentic ceremonial matcha available for take-home purchase. Street parking in Greenpoint is generally available on weekends.

name: Kettl Tea — Greenpoint Flagship
desc: Japanese tea importer's Greenpoint flagship — tasting counter, in-house stone-milled matcha, seasonal wagashi.
longDesc: Kettl's Greenpoint flagship is a serious single-origin Japanese teahouse with a dedicated tasting counter, an in-house Japanese stone mill for fresh matcha, and a seasonal $90 Guided Omakase pairing four loose-leaf teas plus a premium matcha with wagashi handmade daily by Phoebe Ogawa. Walk-ins get matcha, sencha, hojicha, and pastry by-the-pot service in the cafe gallery; the tasting counter is bookable for a more guided flight. About an 18-minute drive up the BQE from Industry City, with weekend street parking around Manhattan Ave / Greenpoint Ave.
notes: Flagship at 70 Greenpoint Ave, Brooklyn NY 11222 (Yelp, Greenpointers). Tasting counter offers curated flights of prized teas plus by-the-pot service of the full catalog (kettl.co/products/tasting-flight). The Class | A Seasonal Guided Omakase Tasting is $90 and includes four loose-leaf teas + one premium stone-milled matcha with seasonal wagashi by Phoebe Ogawa (kettl.co/products/class-a-seasonal-guided-omakase-tasting). Kettl grinds matcha in-house — rare in the US (Tea For Me Please). Crowded on weekends; reservations recommended for the tasting counter and required for the omakase class.

name: Cha-An Teahouse
desc: Hidden 2nd-floor East Village Japanese teahouse with weekend kaiseki-style afternoon tea ($68/pp).
longDesc: Cha-An has served Japanese sweets, savory bento, and a deep tea list from a serene 2nd-floor walk-up on E 9th St since 2004. The weekend-only afternoon tea is a tiered, multi-course set — matcha custard puffs, sakura mochi, inari, egg sandwiches, a tiramisu finisher, and choice of tea — with just 20 seats per session. It's the closest thing to a 'light kaiseki + tea ceremony' experience the East Village offers, and a natural pairing for anyone already in Manhattan for Setsugekka.
notes: Address is 230 E 9th St, 2nd Fl, East Village Manhattan — not Brooklyn; zone tag 'dumbo' reflects the most natural BK-side bridge gateway (Manhattan Bridge) since the enum has no Manhattan option (chaanteahouse.com). Closed Tue/Wed. Weekend afternoon tea is reservation-only and caps at 20 guests/session — book ahead via the site's Sat/Sun slot links (chaanteahouse.com/afternoon-tea). À la carte sweets and savory bento available outside tea service. Weekend parking in East Village is street-only and tough; budget extra time or use a paid lot near Astor Place. Pairs cleanly with Setsugekka (3 blocks away) for a single Manhattan tea-themed half-day (yelp.com).

name: Tea Drunk
desc: Reservation-only gongfu cha teahouse in the East Village — heritage single-origin Chinese teas, multiple steepings.
longDesc: Founded by Shunan Teng (TED-Ed tea historian), Tea Drunk is NYC's most serious Chinese gongfu cha destination: a tiny East Village room where you sit at a wooden tea table and a server brews one rare leaf for you across 6-10 short steepings in small porcelain cups. The seasonal menu rotates every two weeks following the ancient Chinese 24-period lunisolar calendar, drawing from heritage mountains like Wuyi (Dan Cong, Shui Xian) and Yunnan puerh. It sits on the same East Village block as Setsugekka (Japanese chadō at 74 E 7th), making the two a natural Manhattan tea-ceremony crawl that contrasts Chinese and Japanese ritual side by side.
notes: Manhattan venue at 123 E 7th St — justified per task brief because it pairs with Setsugekka (74 E 7th, Japanese chadō) as a single walkable tea-ceremony crawl (edible manhattan, teadrunk.com). Reservation-only seasonal tastings, no walk-ins (teadrunk.com). Menu shifts every two weeks on the Chinese 24-period calendar (cityguideny.com). Yelp shows 'CLOSED' as of Feb 2026 but the official site and founder's LinkedIn confirm reservation tastings are active — recommend calling (917) 573-9936 to confirm before driving in. Parking: street parking around Tompkins Sq is rough on weekends; nearest reliable garages are on E 6th/Avenue A. Drive from Industry City ~22 min off-peak via Hugh L. Carey Tunnel + FDR.

name: Green-Wood Cemetery — Self-Guided Visit + Chapel
desc: 478-acre National Historic Landmark cemetery with Gothic gates, harbor views, and a Warren & Wetmore chapel.
longDesc: Brooklyn's 1838 garden cemetery is a free, drive-in arboretum-museum where you can roam past Tiffany mausoleums, Civil War monuments, and the highest natural point in Brooklyn (Battle Hill) overlooking the harbor. Grab a free map at the 25th Street gate, peek inside the 1911 Warren & Wetmore Neo-Gothic chapel with its 41 stained-glass windows, and—if your visit lands on a Saturday afternoon—add the $30 ADA-accessible Historic Trolley Tour. Vehicle access ends at 4pm on weekends, so arrive by early afternoon.
notes: Free admission and free paper maps at the 5th Ave & 25th St main gate (green-wood.com). Free parking inside on the right-hand side of roads; lot is limited but rarely full on weekend mornings (prked.com). Chapel by Warren & Wetmore (1911), Neo-Gothic with figurative stained glass — just inside the main gate (nylandmarks.org). Optional Historic Trolley Tour ~$30, typically Saturday afternoons, ADA compliant; book ahead via the Green-Wood calendar (destinationaccessible.org). New ARO-designed Weir Greenhouse Welcome Center is now open across from the gate for restrooms/info (architecturalrecord.com).

name: The Evergreens Cemetery
desc: 225-acre 1849 rural-style cemetery in Bushwick with rolling hills, mausoleums, and 500k+ graves; late-afternoon golden hour walk.
longDesc: Designed in 1849 by Andrew Jackson Downing in the rural-cemetery style, Evergreens spans 225 acres of rolling Brooklyn-Queens border land with several thousand trees, ornate Victorian mausoleums, and graves of Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson, jazz saxophonist Lester Young, and painter Martin Heade. The Cooper Avenue gates open Saturday and Sunday only, making weekend a sweet spot for a quiet drive-in photo walk. Important: gates close at 4:30 PM year-round, so 'twilight' here only works in late-fall/winter when sunset falls before close — otherwise treat as a golden-hour stand-in for Green-Wood when after-hours isn't running.
notes: Main entrance: 1629 Bushwick Ave at Conway St; weekend-only Cooper Ave gates on the Queens side give a quieter entry (theevergreenscemetery.org/directions-hours). Free on-street parking is generally available along Bushwick Ave and inside the grounds; visitors drive the loop roads. 225 acres, ~538,000 burials, designed by A.J. Downing in the rural style (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery_of_the_Evergreens). Notables: Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson, Lester Young, Martin Johnson Heade. Caveat: gates close 4:30 PM sharp — true twilight only in Nov-Jan when sunset is ~4:30; rest of year position as golden-hour walk and pair with a separate evening stop nearby (e.g., Bushwick bar or House of Yes-adjacent food).

name: Green-Wood Cemetery Catacombs After-Hours Tour
desc: Rare ticketed walk into the 1850s underground vaults beneath a Gothic Brooklyn cemetery — sells out fast.
longDesc: Green-Wood's After Hours program is the only way the public can see the 30 brick burial vaults set beneath a hill behind locked iron gates, dating to the early 1850s. The roughly two-hour guided walk crosses the cemetery's hilltop landscape, threads past graves of notable New Yorkers, and ends inside the Catacombs corridor itself. Tickets are $30 ($25 members), tours routinely sell out, and the terrain is hilly — bring a flashlight and sturdy shoes.
notes: Enter at the 25th St & 5th Ave Gothic gate; on-site cemetery parking is available for ticketed evening events (Untapped Cities). Tour pairs naturally with the Battle Hill outdoor anchor — Battle Hill is the literal high point above where the catacombs are tucked into the hillside. Members-only free variant available via Untapped New York Insiders (Untapped Cities). Pre-purchase required, no walk-ups.

name: Sunset Park Summit
desc: Free 164-ft hilltop with harbor + Statue of Liberty views, 8 min uphill from Industry City
longDesc: Sunset Park sits atop a 164-foot ridge of the Harbor Hill Moraine — the same glacial spine that gives Green-Wood its elevation, but free, ungated, and closer to Industry City. The 7th Ave & 43rd St corner is the SE entrance nearest the summit lawn, where you get an unobstructed western view of New York Harbor, the Statue of Liberty, lower Manhattan, and (on clear days) the Staten Island hills. Reliable golden-hour pin and a clean alternative when Green-Wood is closed or you don't want to deal with cemetery decorum.
notes: Free 24.5-acre public park; the highest point in the neighborhood at 164 ft on the Harbor Hill Moraine (Wikipedia). View encompasses Manhattan skyline, Statue of Liberty, Staten Island, NJ hills (NYC Parks). Default NYC Parks hours are 6am-1am unless posted otherwise (NYC Parks rules). Recreation center on-site is 8am-10pm weekdays (separate facility). Park entrance closest to summit lawn is 7th Ave & 43rd St (the SE corner, uphill side). Street parking generally available on 6th/7th Ave on weekends. Pairs well with Industry City lunch + Green-Wood as a same-day high-points triptych — same moraine, three different vantage points.

name: Green-Wood Weeping Beech & Valley Water Loop
desc: Walk the canopy tunnel of Larch Ave's weeping beech, then loop down to Valley Water, a glacial kettle pond — all from the 25th St lot.
longDesc: Two of Green-Wood's most cinematic stops, easily strung into one parking session. The Larch Avenue weeping beech (Fagus sylvatica pendula) drapes pendulous, slightly contorted branches across the road to form a living tunnel you walk under. From there, descend to Valley Water — one of four glacial kettle ponds carved by the retreating Wisconsin Ice Sheet ~18,000 years ago — where herons, egrets, and migrating songbirds work the reedy edges (NYC Bird Alliance).
notes: Park free at the main entrance lot, 500 25th St at 5th Ave (Green-Wood). On weekends the Fort Hamilton Pkwy and Prospect Park West (9th Ave/20th St) gates also accept vehicles 8a-4p, but the 25th St lot is the closest to both the Larch Ave beech and Valley Water. Grab a paper map at the gatehouse — pond and tree labels are easier to follow on paper than phone. Best light: late afternoon for backlit beech canopy; early morning for mirror-flat pond reflections and waterfowl. The beech is described as 'the most enchanting' weeping beech in the cemetery, with branches you walk/drive under (green-woodtrees.blogspot.com).

name: Sunset Park Pool & Rec Center Overlook
desc: Bluff-top pool deck and lawn with sweeping skyline, Lady Liberty, and harbor framing minutes uphill from IC.
longDesc: The 1936 WPA-built Sunset Play Center (an NYC Landmark) sits on the highest bluff in Brooklyn at 7th Ave & 43rd St, with the Olympic-size pool deck and surrounding lawns staring straight across the harbor at Lower Manhattan, the Statue of Liberty, and the Bayonne/Staten Island ridge. The pool itself is closed except in summer (late June–Labor Day), but the deck rail, the bleacher steps on the west side, and the lawn just south of the bathhouse are open year-round and give a different, higher-angle framing than the IC rooftop or Bush Terminal pier. The Recreation Center building is currently shut for reconstruction per NYC Parks Capital Tracker, so plan around exterior vantages.
notes: Park is dawn-to-1am daily; pool deck accessible during pool season ~late Jun–Labor Day, 11:00–19:00 with a 14:00–15:00 break (NYC Parks Outdoor Pools). Bathhouse and rec center are closed for reconstruction (NYC Parks Capital Tracker). Best skyline light is golden hour from the western bleachers; for harvester photo variety the lawn just south of the bathhouse gives a clean foreground frame distinct from Bush Terminal Pier and IC roof. Free street parking on 6th/7th Ave and side streets weekends; ADA ramp at 5th Ave entrance. Drive from IC: south on 3rd Ave to 41st, up the hill on 41st to 6th Ave — about 1 mi (sources: NYC Parks; Wikipedia).

name: Kuraichi — Free Sake Tastings
desc: Free Fri/Sat tastings inside IC at NYC's largest Japanese spirits shop — sake, shochu, whisky.
longDesc: Tucked inside Industry City, Kuraichi is the Japan Village–run bottle shop carrying hundreds of sakes plus shochu, awamori, and Japanese whisky. Free walk-in tastings typically run Friday and Saturday afternoons, where staff pour featured bottles (often including the Brooklyn Kura × Japan Village 'Yuzy Crazy' yuzu sake collab) and walk you through origin and brewing method. Pair it with a Brooklyn Kura brewery tour two blocks away for a self-contained sake mini-track.
notes: Inside Industry City at 88 35th St, Bldg 5 (Japan Village floor) (kuraichibk.com). Free tastings 'typically held on Fridays and Saturdays' — no reservation, drop in during store hours (kuraichibk.com/pages/events-calendar). Tasting itself is free; bring cash/card if a bottle catches you (10% off Staff Picks of the Month). Phone (646) 460-3765, IG @kuraichibk for current week's pour list. Pairs perfectly with Brooklyn Kura's brewery tour two blocks east at 68 34th St.

name: Variety Coffee Roasters (Graham Ave Flagship)
desc: Original 2008 Variety flagship; light-roast espresso bar open 7a–9p daily, the latest evening espresso in the cluster.
longDesc: Variety Coffee Roasters' original Graham Avenue flagship opened in 2008 and remains the brand's anchor — a high-ceilinged corner cafe pulling clean, balanced shots and brewed pour-overs from their own East Williamsburg roastery. Critically for evening planning, it runs 7am–9pm seven days a week, making it the only third-wave espresso option in the Williamsburg/Bushwick corridor still serving after a 7:30pm dinner stop. Pairs well as a post-dinner caffeine + walk before driving back to Industry City.
notes: Address 368 Graham Ave, Brooklyn NY 11211 — technically East Williamsburg, not Bushwick proper (the Wyckoff Ave location is the Bushwick one). Hours confirmed Mon–Sun 7am–9pm (source: varietycoffeeroasters.com locations page; cross-checked Yelp). Fills the post-dinner espresso gap that Sey Coffee (closes 6pm) can't cover. Street parking on Graham/Conselyea is plausible on weekend evenings; metered until 7pm weekdays.

name: [CLOSED] Sauvage
desc: PERMANENTLY CLOSED (c. 2020) — former Maison-Premiere-team French bistro at McCarren Park edge.
longDesc: Sauvage operated 2016-2020 at 905 Lorimer St on the Greenpoint/Williamsburg border, opposite McCarren Park, from the same ownership group as Maison Premiere and Sunday in Brooklyn (Joshua Boissy, Krystof Zizka; chef Lisa Giffen). Art Nouveau-styled room with a flagstone patio and raw bar / classic-French menu. Closed during the pandemic and never reopened; the address has since cycled through other tenants. Retained in corpus as historical context for the Greenpoint romantic-bistro lineage — DO NOT route itineraries here.
notes: Confirmed closed: Yelp listing marked CLOSED as of Feb 2026 (yelp.com/biz/sauvage-brooklyn), Gayot states 'THIS RESTAURANT IS CLOSED', Foursquare 'Now Closed', Premiere Enterprises archives it as a past project. Original address: 905 Lorimer St, Brooklyn NY 11222. Team since opened/operates Maison Premiere (Williamsburg) and Sunday in Brooklyn. The romantic-Greenpoint-anchor slot this entry was meant to fill should instead be served by Chez Ma Tante or Lovebirds Wine & Bistro (see enqueue).

name: Diamond Reef (PERMANENTLY CLOSED)
desc: CLOSED: Bed-Stuy tropical cocktail bar from the Attaboy team; landlord terminated lease, no new location yet.
longDesc: Diamond Reef ran for ~7 years at 1057 Atlantic Ave on the Bed-Stuy/Crown Heights border — a tropical, frozen-drink-forward sibling to Manhattan's Attaboy, famous for the frozen Penichillin and a backyard with swinging benches. The building was sold and the lease terminated before a planned 2024 reopening; owners said they'd find a new space but as of late 2025 no replacement venue has opened. Do not route guests here.
notes: Permanently closed; original address 1057 Atlantic Ave, Brooklyn. Confirmed closed on Yelp (Dec 2025) and Foursquare (https://www.yelp.com/biz/diamond-reef-brooklyn-3). Concept was Attaboy-quality cocktails with tropical menu and frozen Penichillin ($12) (Gothamist). Owners said they intend to relocate but no new venue announced. Keep record for corpus history; itinerary builder should filter on 'CLOSED' in desc.

name: Lilia
desc: Missy Robbins' converted-auto-body Italian temple — handmade pastas, wood-fired seafood, James Beard pedigree.
longDesc: Lilia is chef Missy Robbins' flagship Williamsburg restaurant inside a converted auto-body shop at the corner of N. 10th and Union, focused on handcrafted regional Italian pastas, wood-fired seafood, and classic Italian cocktails. It earned three stars from The New York Times and Robbins won James Beard Best Chef NYC in 2018; signatures include mafaldini with pink peppercorn and agnolotti with sheep's milk cheese. Reservations open 30 days out at 9am via Resy and vanish in seconds — bar seats and 4pm Fri/Sat walk-ins are the realistic backdoor.
notes: 567 Union Ave, corner of N. 10th + Union, Brooklyn NY 11211 (Williamsburg/Greenpoint border). Reservations via Resy 30 days out 9am ET, or email reservations@lilianewyork.com; bar walk-ins at 4pm Fri/Sat are the most reliable backdoor (lilianewyork.com). Three NYT stars; Robbins = 2018 James Beard Best Chef NYC (visitbrooklyn.nyc). Pasta-forward menu so vegetarian-friendly though not vegan/GF-flagged. Weekend street parking is realistic on N. 10th/N. 11th — feasible from IC anchor in ~20 min via BQE off weekend peak. Pairs naturally pre- or post-dinner with Maison Premiere (3 min drive south on Bedford) for the same Williamsburg cluster.

name: Kuraichi
desc: NYC's largest curated Japanese sake, shochu and whisky shop, tucked inside Japan Village at IC.
longDesc: Kuraichi (蔵一) is a specialty bottle shop at 88 35th St inside Industry City's Japan Village, two doors from Sunrise Mart. Hundreds of sakes are organized by flavor (dry, fruity, umami-rich), rice variety and prefecture, plus deep shelves of imo/mugi/kome shochu, Japanese whisky and craft spirits. Staff give serious 5-10 minute tastings/walk-throughs, and they collaborate with Brooklyn Kura on yuzu sake exclusives — a tight beverage anchor for the Japan track before or after Sunrise Mart and Brooklyn Kura's taproom.
notes: Established 2019; located inside Japan Village at IC alongside Sunrise Mart and Brooklyn Kura (kuraichibk.com). Inventory spans ginjo/daiginjo/junmai sake, barley/sweet-potato/rice shochu, Japanese whiskies with varied cask finishes; collaborates with Brooklyn Kura + Japan Village on exclusives (kuraichibk.com). Yelp confirms 88 35th St address and Industry City tenancy (industrycity.com/tenants/kuraichi). Park in IC garages on 2nd Ave; the shop sits in the same complex as Sunrise Mart so it pairs as a 30-45 min add-on rather than a separate drive stop.

name: Devoción Williamsburg Flagship
desc: Pitched-skylight Colombian coffee flagship with sunlit courtyard and 35-species plant wall.
longDesc: Devoción's Williamsburg flagship at 148 Grand St is built around a full-length pitched-glass skylight that floods a sunlit courtyard and a floor-to-ceiling living plant wall of 35+ Colombian species. Guests enter via an exposed-brick corridor that opens into the greenery, with a street-visible coffee laboratory used for public cuppings and classes — a far more dramatic photo backdrop than the Industry City branch. Bean-to-cup in roughly 10 days from Colombian farms.
notes: Pitched-roof skylight + courtyard + living plant wall make it the strongest 'photo-first coffee stop' in the Williamsburg track (devocion.com). Coffee lab visible from the street hosts public cuppings/classes (devocion.com). Pair as morning anchor before Smorgasburg or Wythe-corridor galleries. Street parking on Grand/Berry is doable weekend mornings; metered after 9am.

name: Sing Sing Karaoke (Ave A)
desc: East Village private-room karaoke with 15 rooms, BYO food, open till 4am every night.
longDesc: Sing Sing Ave A is the East Village's go-to KTV-style karaoke with 15 private rooms ranging from small couples' rooms to VIP party rooms fitting 15-25 (source: singsingavea.com/rooms). Per-person pricing runs $5/hr before 8pm and $10/hr after, with VIP rooms at $125/$250 per hour; guests can bring outside food for free, and walk-ins are accepted though weekend reservations are recommended. Open every night until 4am, it's the reliable Manhattan backup when JTunes and Goldie's are booked.
notes: Manhattan exception justified by KTV-style private-room operator scarcity in BK; ~22 min drive from IC via Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel or Williamsburg Bridge. 81 Ave A, NYC. Phone (212) 674-0700. Private rooms $5/person/hr pre-8pm, $10/person/hr post-8pm; VIP rooms $125-$250/hr. BYO food allowed at no charge. Reserve weekends via singsingavea.com/reserve (source: yelp.com/biz/sing-sing-ave-a-new-york). Street parking is rough in EV — budget for a garage on E 3rd or Houston.

name: Montero's Bar & Grill
desc: 1939 longshoreman dive on Atlantic Ave with no-cover karaoke Thu–Sat and full nautical patina.
longDesc: Opened in 1939 as a hangout for Brooklyn dockworkers, Montero's is a tiny, low-ceilinged mariner bar at 73 Atlantic Ave still run by the Montero family, with ship lanterns, life rings, and decades of nautical bric-a-brac on every surface. Karaoke runs Thursday, Friday and Saturday nights with no cover, drawing a mixed crowd of regulars and curious first-timers who keep singing well past midnight. Drinks are cheap, the room is small enough that every song feels like a duet with the bar, and it stays open until 4am.
notes: Karaoke Thu/Fri/Sat, no cover, typically kicks off ~9pm and runs late (facebook.com/groups/brooklynkaraokegigs). Cash-friendly old-school dive; expect a small room and a chatty regular base — singing here is participatory, not performative (timeout.com/newyork/bars/monteros). At 73 Atlantic Ave it sits at the Heights/Cobble Hill border with metered + side-street parking on Hicks/Henry that's usually findable on weekends. Open daily 2pm–4am (nyctourism.com/nightlife/monteros). Pairs naturally with a Cobble Hill or Red Hook dinner stop before heading down.

name: Birds of a Feather
desc: Upscale Sichuan from the Cafe China team — numbing-spicy classics in a plant-filled Williamsburg dining room.
longDesc: From the Michelin-starred team behind Manhattan's Cafe China, Birds of a Feather brings serious Sichuan cooking to 191 Grand Street with mapo tofu, dan dan noodles, and dry-fried chicken alongside more creative riffs. The greenery-draped room and well-paced service make it a smart sit-down dinner before bouncing 8-10 minutes east to Mood Ring or other Bushwick bars. Reservations strongly recommended on weekends.
notes: Task said Bushwick but venue is in Williamsburg at 191 Grand St (Yelp, official site).
